title: Stag or hare: how sure must you be?
hook: Both hunters prefer the stag. So why might both settle for a hare?

doesNotKnow: that a better equilibrium needs enough trust: here at least 75% belief that the partner cooperates

misconception: If both prefer the stag outcome, both will hunt stag.
objective: The learner can explain that hunting stag is worth 4 times their confidence in the partner against a sure 3 for hare, so it pays only at 75% confidence or more, and that both-stag and both-hare are each stable, so doubt can lock in the worse outcome.

claims.text: With stag paying 4 if both hunt it and 0 alone, and hare a sure 3, stag is worth 4 times your confidence that the partner hunts stag: 2 at 50%, and it matches hare only at 75%; below 75%, hare is the better bet.
claims.source: Expected value 4p vs 3; 4p >= 3 iff p >= 3/4; 4 x 0.5 = 2. Demo.tsx; re-run in node (ncm-e00). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): 4p vs 3: 4 x 0.5 = 2; 4p = 3 at p = 0.75; THRESH = 3/4 x 100 = 75 in Demo.

claims.text: Each of 'both stag' and 'both hare' is the best reply to itself (both are Nash equilibria); so although both hunters prefer the stag, doubt alone can lock them into hare.
claims.source: Partner stag: stag 4 > hare 3. Partner hare: hare 3 > stag 0. Best-reply check over the 4 cells in node (ncm-e00): (S,S) and (H,H) only. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own best-reply check of the 4 cells: partner S -> S (4 > 3), partner H -> H (3 > 0): (S,S) and (H,H) are the pure Nash equilibria; (S,S) Pareto-dominates. | REWORDED v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): v2 wording; now shown by the two outcome boxes (ticked at 0% and 100%) rather than told alone. Same game-theory content as pass-checked v1. Unverified.

claims.text: The game is called the stag hunt, after an example of Rousseau's.
claims.source: Skyrms, The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure, 2004; Easley and Kleinberg 2010, ch. 6. Fact-checker to confirm. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Search snippets of Skyrms, The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure (Cambridge UP, 2004) publisher/review pages: it starts from the story in Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality. E&K ch. 6 'Games' (stag hunt among coordination games) from own knowledge, confident.

claims.text: The payoffs are invented, in a simplified model with one partner who is as sure of you as you are of them, where only the payoffs matter.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: invented payoffs, one partner' and the reveal's last line. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Chip 'Model: invented payoffs, one partner' and reveal muted line. | REWORDED v2 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): v2 adds the symmetric-belief assumption the outcome boxes use (the partner's best reply at the same confidence equals yours). Unverified.

claims.text: At 0% sure, your best reply is hare, and a partner just as sure of you replies hare too: both hare, 3 each. At 100% it is both stag, 4 each.
claims.source: At p = 0 stag is worth 4 x 0 = 0 < 3, so hare; by symmetry the partner's best reply to a hare-hunter is hare; payoffs (3, 3). At p = 1 stag is worth 4 > 3; payoffs (4, 4). Demo.tsx v2 bestAt(); boxes 'both hare: 3 each' and 'both stag: 4 each'. Builder, 2026-10-14.

recall.question: A joint project pays you 10 if your partner also commits and 0 if they don't; going solo pays a sure 6. How sure of your partner must you be for the project to be worth it?
recall.why: The project is worth 10 times your confidence; it matches the sure 6 at 60%.
